A good TikTok creator brief gives just enough direction to protect your key points and compliance, and not one word more, because over-scripted content is exactly what the algorithm buries. The brief should hand a creator the hook options, the proof points that matter, the offer, and a short do-not-say list, then get out of the way. Here is a template you can copy.

The template

Product: [name, one line on what it is and who it's for]

The one thing to land: [the single most important benefit; if the viewer remembers one thing, this]

Hook options (pick one, make it yours):

  • [hook idea 1]
  • [hook idea 2]
  • [hook idea 3]

See 18 hook formulas for more.

Proof points (use 1 to 2, do not list them all):

  • [benefit with specifics]
  • [result / stat / before-after]

The offer: [discount, bundle, or reason to buy now, and where the link is]

Do NOT say: [banned claims, compliance no-gos, competitor callouts to avoid]

Creative freedom: Everything else is yours. Your style sells better than our script.

Why it is built this way

  • One core message. Cramming five benefits into a 20-second video means none land. Pick the one.
  • Hook options, not a mandate. Different creators land different hooks. Give a menu.
  • A hard do-not-say list. This is where briefs earn their keep, keeping you compliant without micromanaging the rest.
  • Explicit creative freedom. Top creators sell because they sound like themselves. Say so, so they trust you to let them.

The mistake to avoid

The over-detailed brief. Shot lists, required phrases, and word-for-word scripts produce stiff content that underperforms and annoys good creators. The signal that a video was over-briefed is that it feels like an ad, and ad-feeling content is what viewers scroll past. Direction, not dictation.

Sellers see this in the distribution data. A popular r/TikTokshop thread on weak affiliate performance captured the frustration: "My product tagged videos do so poorly compared to my normal videos. Like 10 views to 1000 views respectively" (r/TikTokshop). Some of that is platform mechanics, but the fix creators reach for is the same one a good brief protects: make it feel like content, not a commercial. The more your brief pushes a video toward looking like an ad, the harder that becomes.

Where the brief fits

The brief goes out with seeding and after outreach, once a creator has agreed and has product in hand. It is part of managing a program, not a one-off document.

The takeaway

Brief for the few things that must be right, the message, the proof, the compliance, and hand creators freedom on everything else. That balance is what keeps content native and still on-message.

Want briefs written and creators managed for you? Book a call, or find creators who know how to run with a hook.
